title: MIDILM: Controllable Text-to-MIDI Generation
heroSub: Dual-Path Model for Controllable Symbolic Music Generation

sections.title: Problem
items: Existing Text-to-MIDI models either turn text into a fixed set of musical attributes, which limits what users can ask for, or map text straight to music, which often gets the key, meter, and tempo wrong.
The goal was a model that follows free-form text while keeping the musical structure correct.

sections.title: Approach
items: Dual-path decoder. Text and MIDI tokens share one masked self-attention, then pass through separate feedforward paths: an MLP for text and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for MIDI. Keeping the paths apart stops the two modalities from interfering inside shared weights.

MoE on the music side. MIDI mixes very different token types such as pitch, duration, velocity, and tempo. A router that activates 2 of 8 experts per token gives each type its own capacity at low compute.
Prefix conditioning instead of cross-attention. Text embedded with a pretrained GPT-2 is placed in front of the MIDI sequence, which stabilized training and reduced parameters and compute.

sections.title: My Role
items: As co-first author, ran the main experiments: training the 12-layer decoder on MidiCaps (168K text-MIDI pairs, REMI+ tokens) with cross-entropy plus an MoE load-balancing loss, 100K steps on 4 RTX 3090 GPUs.
Ran ablations that remove modality isolation and MoE routing, to check that each design choice actually helped.
Led the evaluation: semantic and structural metrics (CLAP, CLaMP 3, TB/TBT, CK/CKD, CR) averaged over 10 seeds, and a blind listening test with 15 raters.
Co-wrote the paper and presented the poster at AAAI 2026 in Singapore.

sections.title: Results
items: Beat the strongest baseline on every metric: CLAP +6.07%, tempo bin accuracy 0.40 → 0.97 (+144.77%), key accuracy 0.30 → 0.47.
Listening test MOS 2.49 → 3.23. Removing either modality isolation or MoE lowered every metric, and removing both lowered them the most.

Accepted to the AAAI 2026 Main Track and led to two patents. Its service version CoMIDI was demoed at KSMI 2026, and the team was selected as a top-100 team (of 630) in the AI Champion Program and exhibited at 2025 AI Festa.

title: PixTention: Dynamic Pixel-Level Adapter
period: Image and Vision Computing (IF 4.7), 163:105746 · First author · 2025

sections.title: Problem
items: Stacking several LoRA style adapters on one diffusion model applies every style to the whole image, so styles bleed into regions where they do not belong.
Users also had to pick suitable adapters by hand. This was a follow-up to my earlier LoRA Fusion work, which mixed adapters globally.

sections.title: Approach
items: LoRA adapters stay the unit of style, so new styles can be added without retraining the base model.
Automatic adapter search. A VLM embeds and clusters the adapter library, and a two-stage retrieval picks a matching adapter for each concept in the prompt.
Pixel-level application. Cross-attention maps show which pixels each word in the prompt affects, so each adapter is applied only inside its own concept's region.

sections.title: My Role
items: As first author, led the whole project, from the idea and the three-stage design to implementation, experiments, and writing.
Moved from the single global mix of LoRA Fusion to region masks, because global mixing could not keep one concept's style out of another's region.

sections.title: Results
items: On COCO-Multi and StyleCompose, beat SD v1.5, GlobalMerge, and Stylus with the best CLIP score (27.67), lowest FID (21.97), and best region IoU (0.49).
Ablations showed that semantic clustering, two-stage retrieval, and pixel-level masking each improved the results.
Published in Image and Vision Computing (IF 4.7).

sections.title: Problem
items: A personal study on fitting an LLM into a small memory budget: shrink Qwen3-0.6B to 25 to 33% of its FP16 size while keeping MMLU at 0.36 or above, without using MMLU for calibration.

sections.title: Approach
items: Post-training quantization only, with no retraining, so each idea could be tried quickly on a single GPU.
Started from plain 4-bit RTN and added one technique at a time (clipping search, GPTQ, AWQ, then mixed precision across layers), keeping a change only when it helped.

sections.title: My Role
items: Done alone as a personal study. I implemented each step and compared it with a few well-known alternatives under the same size budget.

sections.title: Results & Takeaways
items: Reached 26.5% of FP16 size (3.77× smaller) with MMLU 0.383 and perplexity 29.72 (FP16: 0.406 and 28.65).
Simple choices mattered most. Group size and clipping range changed the results more than the more complex methods.

One metric is not enough. One model beat FP16 on MMLU while its perplexity got worse. On a 0.6B model, any small change flipped about a fifth of the MMLU answers, so I compared averages over several seeds.
Activations are harder than weights, because a few outlier channels are thousands of times larger than the rest.
